short: Three months of Flanders mud for an advance of about five miles.
full:
The Third Battle of Ypres opened on 31 July 1917 as a British attempt to break out of the salient, take the Passchendaele ridge and reach the Belgian coast, where German submarines were based. A preliminary bombardment of more than four million shells destroyed the drainage of reclaimed farmland, and the wettest August in decades turned the battlefield into liquid mud in which men and pack animals drowned in shell holes.

Plumer's carefully limited bite-and-hold attacks worked well in the drier weather of September, but the rain returned in October. Canadian troops took what was left of Passchendaele village on 6 November and the battle was closed down on the 10th. The advance was about five miles; casualties are usually put between 200,000 and 275,000 on each side. The whole salient was given up without a fight during the German offensive of April 1918. More than the Somme, Passchendaele became the image of the Western Front as futility.
